title: Hay, Necesito and Classroom Talk
bigQuestion: What Spanish do you need to get through the first week of school, from your supply list to asking for help?

story.title: The First Week at a New School
story.kicker: Sofía starts at a bilingual middle school and has one weekend to get ready.
paragraphs: Sofía's family had just moved from Aurora to Little Village in Chicago. On Friday, her new school sent home a supply list written in English and Spanish. Her grandmother, who speaks mostly Spanish, read it out loud at the kitchen table. "Necesitas tres cuadernos, una calculadora y dos carpetas," she said. (You need three notebooks, a calculator and two folders.)

On Saturday they went shopping. Sofía looked at the shelves and tried to name everything. "Hay muchas mochilas," she said. (There are a lot of backpacks.) Her grandmother laughed. "Sí, pero ya tienes una mochila." (Yes, but you already have a backpack.) Sofía checked the list again. She had a backpack and pencils. She still needed the calculator.

On Monday, her homeroom teacher, el señor Fuentes, spoke Spanish most of the morning. "Abran los libros en la página diez," he said. (Open your books to page ten.) Sofía understood abran and libros, but she missed the number. She took a deep breath and raised her hand. "¿Puede repetir, por favor?" (Can you repeat, please?)

El señor Fuentes smiled and said it again, more slowly. After class, he told Sofía, "Asking is the most important skill in any language." By Friday, Sofía knew the names of all her classes, the words on her supply list and five ways to ask for help. She also knew that her question had helped three other students who were too shy to ask.
story.think: Sofía was nervous about asking the teacher to repeat. Why is asking for help a language skill, not a weakness?

lessons.title: One Word: Hay
lessons.mainIdea: Hay means both there is and there are, and it never changes form.
reading: Walk into a classroom and look around. *Hay una pizarra* (There is a board). *Hay veinte pupitres* (There are twenty student desks). The same small word, hay, works for one thing or for many. It is pronounced like the English word eye. The h is silent.

English needs two forms, there is and there are. Spanish needs only one. That makes hay easy, but English speakers sometimes try to make it plural. They say "han" or "hayn" for there are. Those forms are wrong here. Hay stays hay: hay un reloj, hay tres relojes.

To say there is not, put no in front: No hay tiza (There is no chalk). Spanish does not need a word for any or no before the noun in this sentence. No hay papel means There is no paper or There isn't any paper. The word order stays simple: no, then hay, then the thing.

words.d: there is or there are — one form for one thing or many: hay un libro, hay dos libros
the student desk — plural los pupitres
there is not, there are not — no hay tiza, there is no chalk

look.title: Sofía's Homeroom
look.text: Hay una pizarra blanca. (There is a whiteboard.) Hay veinticinco pupitres. (There are twenty-five desks.) Hay dos ventanas grandes. (There are two big windows.) No hay reloj. (There is no clock.) Sofía needs to ask what time it is!
look.prompt: Describe your own classroom in three sentences that start with Hay or No hay.

check.q: How do you say There are three windows?
check.why: Hay means both there is and there are, so it does not change for plural nouns.

check.q: What does No hay papel mean?
check.why: No hay means there is not or there isn't any, so No hay papel means there is no paper.

check.q: How is hay pronounced?
choices: Like hay in English, with an h
check.why: The h in Spanish is silent, and ay sounds like the English word eye.

lessons.title: Hay With Un, Una or Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: After hay, use un, una, a number or no article, but not el or la.
reading: Hay introduces something new. You are telling someone that a thing exists in a place. That is why hay goes with *un* or una, a number, or words like muchos (many): hay una computadora, hay muchos libros. These words introduce things the listener has not heard about yet.

A very common mistake is "Hay el libro en la mesa." That sentence mixes two ideas. If you mean a book, say Hay un libro en la mesa (There is a book on the table). If you mean the specific book you were talking about, Spanish uses a different verb, estar: El libro está en la mesa (The book is on the table).

Plural nouns after hay can also stand with no article at all. Hay lápices en la caja means There are pencils in the box. This is like English, where you can also say there are pencils without some. Just remember the rule of thumb: hay plus el or la is almost never right.

words.d: many, a lot of — hay muchos libros, hay muchas sillas
the computer — feminine; some countries also say el ordenador
the box — feminine; hay lápices en la caja

look.title: Right or Wrong?
look.text:
Hay una computadora en la mesa. ✓ (a computer)
Hay muchas sillas. ✓ (many chairs)
Hay lápices en la caja. ✓ (pencils, no article)
Hay la computadora en la mesa. ✗ → La computadora está en la mesa. (The computer is on the table.)
look.prompt: Fix this sentence two ways: Hay el mapa en la pared.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Hay el reloj en la pared.
Hay la reloj en la pared.
Hay los reloj en la pared.
Hay un reloj en la pared.
check.why: Hay introduces something new, so it goes with un, una or a number, not el or la.

check.q: You want to say the specific map is on the wall. Which sentence works?
choices: Hay el mapa en la pared.
El mapa hay en la pared.
El mapa está en la pared.
check.why: For a specific thing that is in a place, Spanish uses estar: El mapa está en la pared.

check.q: What does Hay muchas mochilas mean?
choices: There are a lot of backpacks.
check.why: Hay means there are, and muchas means many or a lot of.

lessons.title: Asking ¿Qué hay en…?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿Qué hay en…? to find out what is in a place, and ¿Cuántos hay? to ask how many.
reading: Sofía's grandmother opened the new backpack and asked, "*¿Qué hay en* la mochila?" (What is in the backpack?) Sofía answered, "Hay un cuaderno y dos lápices." The question uses qué (what) plus hay plus en (in or on) and a place. The answer starts with hay too.

To ask how many, use ¿Cuántos hay? for masculine nouns and ¿Cuántas hay? for feminine ones. ¿Cuántos libros hay? means How many books are there? ¿Cuántas sillas hay? means How many chairs are there? Notice the question word matches the noun, just like an adjective does.

Remember the upside-down question mark at the start: ¿. English speakers often forget it. Also remember the accent on qué and cuántos in questions. Without the accent, que and cuantos are different words. The accent tells the reader this is a real question word.

words.d: What is there in…? What is in…? — ¿Qué hay en la mochila?
how many? — matches the noun: ¿cuántos libros?, ¿cuántas sillas?
in, on or at — en la mesa, on the table; en la caja, in the box

look.title: What Is in Sofía's Backpack?
look.cite: Example backpack contents from the story, invented for practice
look.prompt: Ask and answer in Spanish: ¿Cuántos lápices hay? ¿Cuántas carpetas hay?

check.q: How do you ask How many chairs are there?
check.why: Silla is feminine, so the question word is cuántas, and there are is hay.

check.q: What does ¿Qué hay en la caja? mean?
check.why: Qué means what, hay means there is, and en la caja means in the box.

check.q: Which question is written correctly?
check.why: A Spanish question needs ¿ at the start, ? at the end and the accent on cuántos.

sections.title: What I Need and What I Have

lessons.title: Necesito: I Need
lessons.mainIdea: Necesito means I need; it can come before a noun or before a verb in its base form.
reading: Sofía read her supply list and said, "*Necesito* una calculadora" (I need a calculator). Necesito comes from necesitar (to need), a regular -ar verb. Drop -ar and add endings: necesito (I need), necesitas (you need), necesita (he, she or you formal need). You can use these three forms right away.

Necesito can come before a noun: necesito un lápiz. It can also come before another verb in its base form, the infinitive, which ends in -ar, -er or -ir: Necesito estudiar (I need to study). Necesito ir al baño (I need to go to the bathroom). English adds to. Spanish does not.

A common mistake is "Necesito a estudiar," with an extra a, copied from English to. Leave it out. Another mistake is using the -o ending for everyone: "Tú necesito." Match the ending to the person. Tú necesitas, Sofía necesita.

words.d: to need — a regular -ar verb: necesito, necesitas, necesita
the calculator — feminine
the infinitive — the base form of a verb, ending in -ar, -er or -ir: estudiar

look.title: The Supply List Walk-Through
look.text:
necesitar → drop -ar → necesit- → add the ending.
yo necesito una calculadora (I need a calculator).
tú necesitas dos carpetas (you need two folders).
ella necesita estudiar (she needs to study).
No extra word for to: necesito estudiar, not necesito a estudiar.
look.prompt: Tell a partner two things you need for school and one thing you need to do tonight.

check.q: How do you say I need to study?
check.why: Necesito goes straight to the infinitive. Spanish does not add a word for to.

check.q: Which form fits: Tú ___ un bolígrafo.
check.why: With tú, a regular -ar verb takes -as: tú necesitas.

check.q: What does Sofía necesita dos carpetas mean?
check.why: Necesita means he or she needs, so the sentence means Sofía needs two folders.

lessons.title: Tengo: I Have
lessons.mainIdea: Tengo means I have; tener is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene.
reading: Sofía's grandmother pointed at the backpack. "Ya *tienes* una mochila." (You already have a backpack.) Sofía answered, "Sí, *tengo* una mochila." (Yes, I have a backpack.) These forms come from tener (to have). Tener is irregular, which means it does not follow the normal pattern.

Look at the forms: tengo (I have), tienes (you have), tiene (he, she or you formal have), tenemos (we have), tienen (they or you all have). The yo form has a surprise g. In three forms the e becomes ie. Only tenemos keeps the plain e from tener. Spain also uses tenéis for you all.

Learners often say "teno" or "tieno" for I have. Both are wrong. Memorize tengo as a word by itself. You can also say what you do not have: No tengo calculadora (I don't have a calculator). In negative sentences like this, speakers often drop un or una.

words.d: to have — an irregular verb: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen
I have — the yo form of tener, with a g: tengo un lápiz
you have (tú) — ¿Tienes un bolígrafo? Do you have a pen?

look.title: Borrowing a Pen
look.text:
Sofía: ¿Tienes un bolígrafo? (Do you have a pen?)
Diego: Sí, tengo dos. (Yes, I have two.)
Sofía: Gracias. Yo no tengo bolígrafo hoy. (Thanks. I don't have a pen today.)
Diego: No hay problema. (No problem.)
look.prompt: Ask a classmate if they have three different school supplies, using ¿Tienes…?

check.q: How do you say I have a notebook?
check.why: Tener is irregular. The yo form is tengo, with a g.

check.q: Which form fits: Nosotros ___ clase de ciencias.
check.why: The nosotros form keeps the plain e from tener: tenemos.

check.q: Diego says, Sí, tengo dos. What does he mean?
check.why: Tengo means I have, so tengo dos means I have two.

lessons.title: The Supply List
lessons.mainIdea: Learn school supplies with their articles so you can ask for, buy and borrow them.
reading: Sofía's supply list had eight items. Each one is a noun you can use with hay, necesito and tengo. *El cuaderno* (the notebook), la carpeta (the folder), *el bolígrafo* (the pen), el lápiz (the pencil), la regla (the ruler), la goma (the eraser), las tijeras (the scissors) and la calculadora (the calculator).

Some supplies have more than one name across the Spanish-speaking world. A pen is el bolígrafo in many places and la pluma in Mexico. An eraser can be la goma or el borrador. None of these is wrong. Heritage speakers can use the word their family uses. In class, just know that several words may point to the same object.

Notice las tijeras. English says scissors, a plural word for one tool. Spanish also uses a plural here: Necesito las tijeras. When you shop, you might see a price tag. Prices below are only examples. If a notebook costs two dollars, three notebooks cost six dollars: tres cuadernos, seis dólares.

words.d: the notebook — masculine; plural los cuadernos
the pen — also la pluma in Mexico; both are correct
the ruler — feminine; it also means the rule
the scissors — a plural word for one tool, as in English

look.title: Shopping for the List
look.cite: Example prices invented for practice, not real store prices
look.prompt: Sofía needs tres cuadernos and dos carpetas. How much do they cost together at these example prices?

check.q: Which item is NOT a school supply?
check.why: La ventana is the window. The others are the ruler, the notebook and the pen.

check.q: At the example prices, a notebook costs $2. How much do tres cuadernos cost?
check.why: Three notebooks at two dollars each cost three times two, which is six dollars: seis dólares.

check.q: Your cousin from Mexico says pluma for pen. What should you think?
choices: Pluma is wrong; only bolígrafo is right
Pluma is a real word for pen in Mexico
check.why: Many supplies have regional names. Pluma is a common word for pen in Mexico, and bolígrafo is common elsewhere.

lessons.title: School Subjects
lessons.mainIdea: School subjects are nouns with articles, and many look like their English names.
reading: On Monday, Sofía got her schedule. It listed her classes: *las matemáticas* (math), *la historia* (history), *las ciencias* (science), el inglés (English), el español (Spanish), el arte (art) and la educación física (P.E.). Many look like the English words, which helps you guess.

Look at the articles. Matemáticas and ciencias are plural in Spanish, even though math and science are singular in English. So you say las matemáticas and las ciencias. Languages like inglés and español are masculine and are not capitalized in Spanish. English capitalizes English. Spanish writes inglés with a small i.

To name a class, you can say la clase de plus the subject: la clase de historia (history class). Tengo clase de ciencias means I have science class. In that phrase, Spanish does not use an article after de. It is clase de arte, not clase de el arte.

words.d: math — a plural noun in Spanish: las matemáticas
history — also means story
science — plural in Spanish: la clase de ciencias
English (the language) — masculine and written with a small i

look.title: Sofía's Schedule Card
look.text:
1. las matemáticas
2. el inglés
3. las ciencias
4. el almuerzo (lunch)
5. la historia
6. el español
7. la educación física
Sofía tells her grandmother: "Tengo clase de historia después del almuerzo." (I have history class after lunch.)
look.prompt: Write your own schedule in Spanish with the article for each class.

check.q: Which is the correct way to write Spanish class in Spanish?
check.why: Clase is feminine, and names of languages are not capitalized in Spanish: la clase de español.

check.q: Which article goes with matemáticas?
check.why: Matemáticas is a feminine plural noun, so it takes las.

check.q: What does Tengo clase de ciencias mean?
check.why: Tengo means I have, and clase de ciencias means science class.

lessons.title: When Is the Class?
lessons.mainIdea: Say a la una or a las plus a number to tell what time a class starts.
reading: Sofía's friend Diego asked, "¿A qué hora es la clase de arte?" (What time is art class?) Sofía looked at her schedule. "*A las* dos." (At two.) To say at a time, use a las and the number: a las nueve (at nine), a las once (at eleven).

One o'clock is different, because una is singular. Say *a la una* (at one), not a las una. This is the same agreement rule you learned for articles. Una is one hour, so the article is la. Every other hour is more than one, so the article is las.

You can add a subject to make a full answer: Tengo matemáticas a las ocho (I have math at eight). If a class starts at 8:30, add y media (and a half): a las ocho y media. A class from 8:30 to 9:15 lasts 45 minutes, so it is shorter than one hour.

words.d: At what time? — ¿A qué hora es la clase?
at (a time, two o'clock or later) — a las dos, a las once
at one o'clock — la because una is singular

look.title: Comparing Schedules
look.text:
Diego: ¿A qué hora es tu clase de historia? (What time is your history class?)
Sofía: A la una. ¿Y tu clase de arte?
Diego: A las dos y media. (At two thirty.)
Sofía: ¡Yo también tengo arte a las dos y media! (I also have art at two thirty!)
look.prompt: Ask a partner what time two of their classes are, and answer about yours.

check.q: How do you say at one o'clock?
check.why: Una is singular, so you use la: a la una.

check.q: Sofía says, Tengo matemáticas a las ocho y media. When is her math class?
check.why: A las ocho means at eight, and y media adds half an hour: 8:30.

check.q: Which question asks what time a class is?
check.why: ¿A qué hora…? asks at what time something happens.

lessons.title: Commands You Will Hear
lessons.mainIdea: Teachers give class commands in the ustedes form, which often ends in -en or -an.
reading: El señor Fuentes said, "*Abran* los libros" (Open your books), to the whole class. A command tells someone to do something. When a teacher talks to the whole group, the command uses the ustedes (you all) form. For -ar verbs, it usually ends in -en: *Escuchen* (Listen), Miren (Look). For -er and -ir verbs, it ends in -an: Abran (Open), Escriban (Write), Lean (Read).

The endings look flipped. Escuchar is an -ar verb, but its command ends in -en. Abrir is an -ir verb, but its command ends in -an. This swap is a real pattern, not a mistake. You will learn why in later units. For now, learn these commands by ear and by action.

Some commands you will hear every day are Siéntense (Sit down), Levanten la mano (Raise your hand), Saquen una hoja de papel (Take out a sheet of paper) and Repitan (Repeat). The teacher may also speak to one student with a tú command: Abre el libro, Escucha. Both forms ask for the same action.

words.d: open (you all) — a class command from abrir: Abran los libros
listen (you all) — a class command from escuchar
sit down (you all) — a class command; the accent keeps the stress on sién
take out (you all) — from sacar: Saquen una hoja de papel

look.title: Simon Says, Spanish Style
look.text:
El señor Fuentes: Levanten la mano. (Everyone raises a hand.)
El señor Fuentes: Siéntense. (Everyone sits.)
El señor Fuentes: Saquen un lápiz. (Everyone takes out a pencil.)
El señor Fuentes: Escriban su nombre. (Everyone writes their name.)
Listen for the verb, then act it out.
look.prompt: Take turns giving three class commands to your group. Can they act each one out?

check.q: The teacher says Escuchen. What should the class do?
check.why: Escuchen comes from escuchar, to listen. It is the ustedes command form.

check.q: Which command means Open the books, said to the whole class?
check.why: Abran is the ustedes command of abrir, used for a whole group.

check.q: Why does escuchar give Escuchen, with an e?
choices: Ustedes commands of -ar verbs switch to -en
check.why: For ustedes commands, -ar verbs take -en and -er/-ir verbs take -an.

lessons.title: Asking for Help
lessons.mainIdea: Use short, polite questions like ¿Puede repetir, por favor? to keep learning when you are lost.
reading: When Sofía missed the page number, she asked, "*¿Puede repetir, por favor?*" (Can you repeat, please?) Puede is the usted form of poder (to be able to), the polite way to talk to a teacher. You can also say Más despacio, por favor (More slowly, please) or No entiendo (I don't understand).

When you know the English word but not the Spanish one, ask *¿Cómo se dice…?* (How do you say…?). ¿Cómo se dice scissors en español? When you hear a Spanish word you do not know, ask ¿Qué significa…? (What does … mean?). ¿Qué significa tijeras?

Use usted, not tú, with most teachers. Saying "¿Puedes repetir?" to a teacher is understood, but it can sound too casual in many schools. Some students worry that asking questions makes them look lost. In fact, these questions show you are working in Spanish. They keep the conversation going instead of switching to English.

words.d: Can you repeat, please? — polite usted form, good for teachers
How do you say…? — ¿Cómo se dice pencil en español?
What does … mean? — ¿Qué significa pupitre?
I don't understand. — from entender, to understand

look.title: Five Lifelines
look.text:
1. ¿Puede repetir, por favor? (Can you repeat, please?)
2. Más despacio, por favor. (More slowly, please.)
3. No entiendo. (I don't understand.)
4. ¿Cómo se dice ___ en español? (How do you say ___ in Spanish?)
5. ¿Qué significa ___? (What does ___ mean?)
look.prompt: Pick the lifeline you would use if you know the word ruler in English but not in Spanish. Say the full question.

check.q: You know the word ruler in English but not in Spanish. What do you ask?
check.why: ¿Cómo se dice…? asks how to say an English word in Spanish.

check.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a teacher to repeat?
check.why: Puede is the usted form, which is polite, and por favor adds please.

check.q: What does No entiendo mean?
check.why: Entiendo comes from entender, to understand, so No entiendo means I don't understand.

review.q: How do you say There are twenty desks?
review.why: Hay means both there is and there are and never changes form.

choices: Hay el libro en la mesa.
Hay una libro en la mesa.
Hay un libro en la mesa.
Hay libro un en la mesa.
review.why: Hay goes with un or una, and libro is masculine, so it is hay un libro.

review.q: How do you say I have a calculator?
review.why: The yo form of tener is tengo, and calculadora is feminine, so it takes una.

review.q: How do you say I need to study?
review.why: Necesito goes directly before the infinitive, with no word for to.
Ciencias is feminine plural, so the article is las.

review.q: The teacher says Saquen una hoja de papel. What should you do?
choices: Take out a sheet of paper
review.why: Saquen is the ustedes command of sacar, to take out.
¿Qué significa…? asks the meaning of a word.

review.q: Your history class is at one o'clock. What do you say?
review.why: One o'clock is singular, so the phrase is a la una.
